utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. That's fine. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Mr. Vishi, drawing your attention to the photograph that has just appeared on the screen, do you know who that person is?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: Yes. I know the person. He is Hajrush Qorri.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: And when was the last time you saw Mr. Qorri alive?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: Before the 25th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: And where did you obtain this photograph?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: The photograph was taken from the same person, and he was photographed on the same date, on the 26th of May, after the Serbian forces withdrew from the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: May I have page 5 of the same exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Drawing your attention to the person shown in that photograph, do you know that person?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: Yes. I recognise him. He is Arben Qorri, Hajrush Qorri's son, the one we saw before in the picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Thank you. May I have page 1 of that exhibit? And who is depicted in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: The girl in the middle is Fetija Qorri [phoen]. She is the daughter of the deceased Hajrush Qorri. She was very young when she was killed alongside her mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Do you know when she was killed?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: She was killed on the 25th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Have you personally seen her alive since the 25th of May?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: No. I couldn't because she was killed on the 25th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Does that photograph -- is that photograph a reasonable approximation of her age and appearance when she was killed?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: She was about seven to nine years old. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Does the photograph show about the way she looked when you saw her back in May?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: Yes. Because this photograph was taken when she was alive. She used to be a pupil in the school where I worked, and I knew her, and also she is an niece of my cousin's.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Scully, there was a video rejected by the Court in the Milosevic trial and it seems to have related to the same issue as you've just been dealing with. Do you know if there is a link between the video and these photographs?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: They are basically one and the same except the video is a lot longer and we just opted not to show it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But that's all it would do is demonstrate the identity of individuals who are now deceased or the actual bodies of the now deceased?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In fact, it would be the bodies, it wouldn't be -- the very last example you've given us wouldn't be on the video?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: The last example is not on the video. The video was taken I believe at the end of May 1999 and just shows damage to the village and the bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The order will be General Lazarevic, General Lukic, General Pavkovic, General Ojdanic, Mr. Sainovic and Mr. Milutinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Cepic, your hour has come.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, Your Honour, yet again.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vishi, good afternoon, my name is Djuro Cepic, an attorney-at-law, part of the team of Defence for General Lazarevic. You gave this statement on the 18th of October, 1999, to OTP investigators, and I suppose you understood that statement, you signed it, and accepted it as something that you have stated; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Then on the 7th of May, 2002, you testified in the Milosevic trial before this very Tribunal, is that so?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: On both occasions, you describe the events on the 5th of May, 1999, when three persons in camouflage uniform kidnapped Sylejman Gurri. And then on page -- or transcript 4472 in the Milosevic trial, you describe that you saw those people wearing camouflage uniforms only briefly, for just a second. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: I saw them briefly because they had taken positions, but when Sylejman Gurri --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you couldn't see whether they had any facial hair; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: I saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: But you couldn't see exactly what they looked like in detail.

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: I did see them in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Were you able to observe whether any of them had a beard or moustache?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: No. No beard or moustaches. Just one of them was tall, but they did not have long hair. But I recognised this person he was different from the others because he had white hair and white eyes. He was like an albino.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: So they were between 30 and 50; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: One of them could have been younger.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: As you stated previously, they didn't wear any hats?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: At the moment when they stood up, they did not wear -- they were not wearing hats.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And you didn't see any insignia on them, is that so?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: I did not see any insignia. I just saw camouflage uniforms and Kalashnikovs in their hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Further on in your statement, you mention that Mr. Ramadan Lami was buried in Stari Kacanik, old Kacanik. Can you tell me where exactly at what cemetery?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: I don't know that. He was buried by some of my friends. I know that he was buried in Kacanik i Vjeter.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. We now come to the 25th of May, around 3.30 a.m. You stated that the village was surrounded. You came to the school where the villagers had gathered, and you told them to make a convoy and leave the village, is that so?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You were the main person in the village at that moment; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: Yes. I was kind of leader in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: How do you explain the fact that you, as a somewhat younger man, were assigned that position, although there were some other men in the village who were older than you?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: I can explain that because a leader in a village is never elected because of his age. It was someone who people trusted. That was the person who usually got elected.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At that moment, being dark still, you were unable to see exactly who had surrounded you. Once the convoy set out, you took to the mountains and you hid there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: The truth was that at that time we had organised ourselves to protect the village in a way. My brother was one of the guards, along with a cousin. They informed me that the village was surrounded. Then after that, I informed the people that we are surrounded and that we must find a way out of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Prior to that, you had information that there was fighting between the KLA and the police in the village of Stagovo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: That happened on the 21st of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And you knew that there was fighting in all the nearby villages between the KLA and the police such as Sopotnica, Kovacevac, Bicevac, Nika and Doganovic; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: No. We did not have that information because, in fact, no fighting took place between the KLA and the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You took to the mountains and from there you were able to observe the convoy leave. You mentioned that your brother drove the first tractor in the convoy and that he was stopped by some soldiers. And as it is stated in your statement, it was about one kilometre from your village but I believe you at that point were further up, more than one kilometre.

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: No. That is not correct. As the crow flies, we were not more than one kilometre away. And when the convoy stopped it was about one kilometre from the centre of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And from that distance, you couldn't clearly make out the uniforms worn by those people, you could only see their colour; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: That is correct. I couldn't see very clearly the uniforms but I could see that they were military uniforms. And afterwards, my brother told me everything about the uniforms and about what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did you know that local Serbs also wore green camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: There was no reason for the local Serbs to wear uniforms. Only the soldiers wore uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: So today you are trying to tell us that only the military wore uniforms. Is this what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: If you go by the book, only the army is supposed to wear uniforms. The civilians usually wear civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You will agree with me that your recollection was far better back in 1999 when you gave the first statement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: I didn't understand what you mean by this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could you remember those events better at that time, better than now, seven years later?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: No, no. I remember things accurately now and then, because I'm telling only the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Therefore, when you gave your statement back in 1999, your recollection was very good, as well as when you testified against Slobodan Milosevic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: Yes. Because these are things that will live with us forever, because we suffered very much as a result of these events.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Since your recollection was so good, how come in the past seven years you never mentioned Pragas and APCs? How do you explain that fact? In the seven years, you never mentioned what you told this Chamber today.

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: I didn't say this earlier because at the time that I gave my statement before the investigators of The Hague Tribunal, at that time --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Sir, you had seven years on your hands to correct that and it is just today that you've introduced new details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, you did not give the witness there the opportunity to explain. He started by saying, "I didn't say this earlier because at the time that I gave my statement before the investigators of The Hague Tribunal, at that time --" and then you cut him off. Now, please continue, Mr. Vishi, and explain what you were going to tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to say that at that time that I gave the statement, there were other persons who gave statements, too, from my village, and I personally wanted to concentrate only on the kidnapping. But when I saw that the other witnesses were not invited to testify, and the fact is that I know what I'm saying, what I'm mentioning now, I wanted to point out now these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vishi, how do you know what others testified about?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: I am not saying that I know what they wanted to say, but I do know what occurred in the village. This is what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The explanation he gave, Mr. Cepic, was that when he saw that they were not invited to testify, that he expanded his statement. He's not claiming to have inside knowledge of what they said, I don't think.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vishi, do you know that on 25 May 1999, the day that we are talking about right now, in all the villages around your village, there was fighting between the KLA on the one side and the police on the other? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: No. No fighting took place between the KLA and the Serbian forces. There were no fighting. The case was that the Serbian forces attacked at will.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't have any more questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cepic. Just give me a moment. Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe in so far as the testimony for today we have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Don't please sound so surprised. Mr. Ackerman. Sorry, Mr. Aleksic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We also don't have any questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scully.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions, only to move to admit the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Well, Mr. Vishi, that brings your evidence to an end. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal yet again to give it. And you're now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. And I wish you all the best and good health.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: I fear it falls to me to tell you we have nothing else for the day, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I was going to say I'm glad I'm not you, Mr. Hannis, but ... It would be churlish, though, not to acknowledge that there has been a very expeditious conduct of business today, and I suspect at all hands there is an element of surprise that we've reached this stage so quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think that's fair to say, Your Honour. It was not readily foreseeable based on our experience up to this date. We have four more witnesses for this week. The first one tomorrow I anticipate will take longer than either of these two. But the remaining three are similar in nature, I think, to the two that we had today. If that's the case, we may run short again this week. I sent an e-mail, we are making some efforts to see if we can get some additional people here this week. I welcome this trend, if indeed it is the beginning of a trend, and we will try to adjust our scheduling accordingly. We did have in mind the proposed schedule you talked about, with half an hour or direct and redirect and 90 minutes for cross for the week of the 25th, and I have tried to schedule a number of witnesses based on that for that week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm beginning to think we've been far too generous. No. I welcome the trend that takes a lead from that sort of indication given by the Bench, the Bench itself having tried to give an indication based on experience over the initial weeks of the trial. And as we move forward, hopefully the real areas of controversy will be those on which we concentrate and the marginal areas will be the ones that we abandon in the, I think, interests of everyone. So it looks as though we can now adjourn until 2.15 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 20th day of September 2006, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 5.11 p.m.,
